headline: Trump made the Oval Office a national monument.
summary: President Trump signed a proclamation on Thursday making the Oval Office and the Cabinet Room a national monument, two days after voters handed Congress to the Democrats. He said nobody will be allowed to touch it. The order itself lets any president redecorate. A preservation lawyer told the BBC it is legally meaningless.

cover_question.q: Can one president bind the next one?

cover_answer: No. The order itself says the next one can redecorate.
table_question: Should you get a say in what the next person does with your room?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: The president works in a room shaped like an egg, called the Oval Office. He put a lot of gold on its walls, and on Thursday he signed a paper saying the room is a national monument, like a park nobody is allowed to wreck. The next president can still pick the furniture. The grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: The egg-shaped room is the picture and the gold is the detail they will hold. At six they reason from what they can see, so the room carries it and the law can wait.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script gives them the room: egg-shaped, gold on the walls, a paper that says don't wreck it. Nothing is broken and nobody is in trouble, which is the only stake this age has. Expect "can I see it?" Yes, there are pictures, and it is very gold.

8-12.script: Trump filled the Oval Office with gold trim. On Thursday he signed an order calling it a national monument, the label used for national parks. But the order lets any president redecorate, and knocking down walls needs Congress. A do-not-touch sign, signed by the kid who's moving out.
8-12.why: Order, label, loophole: a chain, and at ten they find the loophole themselves.
8-12.why_long: A ten-year-old is working out rules and whether the people who make them follow them, so the script hands over the chain: an order, the park label, and the loophole that lets the next president redecorate anyway. Expect "so what does it actually do?" Honest answer: on paper, almost nothing. That is the lesson.

13-17.script: Trump made his own office a national monument two days after his party lost Congress. Can one president bind the next? The order lets any president redecorate; a lawyer called it legally meaningless. Second: that lawyer says Trump is suing to weaken rules on other old buildings. Preservation, or him?
13-17.why: A rule written by the one it benefits. At 16 they can ask who it's for.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things: a president can create a national monument, and this one declared his own office one two days after losing Congress. The script sets the lawyer's 'legally meaningless' against Trump's 'symbol of our country'. Expect "isn't this just vanity?" Say what you think and let them argue back.

5-7.q: Can he keep his office forever?
5-7.a: No. The next president moves in and can change the furniture. The room stays.

8-12.a: Protected land or a building, like a national park.

8-12.q: So nobody can change the Oval Office now?
8-12.a: Decor, yes. The order lets any president pick the furniture.

13-17.q: Can one president bind the next one?
13-17.a: Not with this. The order lets any president redecorate.

13-17.q: Why do it two days after losing Congress?
13-17.a: He called it a symbol of the country.
